children.text: Image of a charge in a metallic object

A point charge \(q\) lies at distance \(d>R\) from the centre of a grounded metal sphere of radius \(R\). Outside the sphere, its induced surface-charge potential can be replaced by an image charge \(q^{\prime}\) at distance \(d^{\prime}\) from the centre on the line towards \(q\). The image representation is valid only on and outside the surface. Use vacuum permittivity \(\epsilon_0\).
What is the potential on the sphere?
Find the force on the charge and state whether it is repulsive.

nodes.alt: Original charge q, grounded sphere and point A behind it, with distances d and r.

children.text: Point A is beyond the sphere on the axis, on the opposite side from \(q\), at distance \(r>d+R\) from \(q\). Take positive axial direction from \(q\) towards A. Find the signed field component at A.
For \(r\gg d\), expand the axial field through the first correction of order \(r^{-3}\), using \((1+u)^{-2}\simeq1-2u\).
In what limit is the field at A completely screened?

nodes.alt: Original charged pendulum near the grounded sphere, labelled R, L, l and alpha.

children.text: A charge of mass \(m\) is suspended by a thread of length \(L\) from a point at distance \(l\) from the centre, with \(l-L>R\). Ignore gravity and wall electrostatics. The thread makes angle \(\alpha\) with the line from the support towards the centre. Find the force magnitude and draw its direction.
Find the component perpendicular to the thread for \(\alpha>0\).
Find the energy of interaction between \(q\) and all induced surface charges.
Find the mutual interaction energy among the induced charges.
Find the total electrostatic interaction energy.

statement.text:
Image of a charge in a metallic object
A point charge \(q\) lies at distance \(d>R\) from the centre of a grounded metal sphere of radius \(R\). Outside the sphere, its induced surface-charge potential can be replaced by an image charge \(q^{\prime}\) at distance \(d^{\prime}\) from the centre on the line towards \(q\). The image representation is valid only on and outside the surface. Use vacuum permittivity \(\epsilon_0\).
1a. Sphere potential
What is the potential on the sphere?
1b.q. Image charge
Find \(q^{\prime}\) in terms of \(q,d,R\).
1b.d. Image position
Find \(d^{\prime}\).
1c. Force magnitude
Find the force on the charge and state whether it is repulsive.
2a. Field behind the sphere

Point A is beyond the sphere on the axis, on the opposite side from \(q\), at distance \(r>d+R\) from \(q\). Take positive axial direction from \(q\) towards A. Find the signed field component at A.
2b. Far field
For \(r\gg d\), expand the axial field through the first correction of order \(r^{-3}\), using \((1+u)^{-2}\simeq1-2u\).
2c. Complete screening
In what limit is the field at A completely screened?
3a. Pendulum force

A charge of mass \(m\) is suspended by a thread of length \(L\) from a point at distance \(l\) from the centre, with \(l-L>R\). Ignore gravity and wall electrostatics. The thread makes angle \(\alpha\) with the line from the support towards the centre. Find the force magnitude and draw its direction.
3b. Tangential force magnitude
Find the component perpendicular to the thread for \(\alpha>0\).
3c. Small-oscillation angular frequency
Find the small-oscillation angular frequency.
4a. External-induced interaction energy
Find the energy of interaction between \(q\) and all induced surface charges.
4b. Induced-charge mutual energy
Find the mutual interaction energy among the induced charges.
4c. Total interaction energy
Find the total electrostatic interaction energy.

children.text: Image of a charge in a metallic object

At every surface point the two potentials cancel if \(q\to q\), \(q^{\prime}=-qR/d\), and \(d^{\prime}=R^2/d\). These follow either from the two axial points or from the general surface-distance ratio.
The image gives an attractive force towards the centre with magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rd}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)^2}.\]
The real-charge field points towards A for positive \(q\), while the image field opposes it. Thus \[E_A=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac1{r^2}-\frac{R/d}{(r-d+R^2/d)^2}\right].\]

The total charge seen at leading order is \(q+q^{\prime}=q(1-R/d)\). Therefore \[E_A\simeq\frac{q(1-R/d)}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}.\] Expanding one order further gives a correction \(-2qR(1-R^2/d^2)/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\).
Only in the limit \(d\to R^+\), when the real and image charges coincide at the surface with opposite signs.

The charge-centre distance is \(s=\sqrt{l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha}\). The force points towards the sphere centre and has magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rs}{4\pi\epsilon_0(s^2-R^2)^2}.\] Draw this central force at the bob.
Geometry gives \(\sin\gamma=l\sin\alpha/s\). The restoring-component magnitude is \[F_\perp=\frac{q^2Rl\sin\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0(l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha-R^2)^2}.\]
Linearize \(mL\ddot\alpha=-F_\perp\). The result is \[\omega=\frac{|q|}{(l-L)^2-R^2}\sqrt{\frac{Rl}{4\pi\epsilon_0mL}}.\] The ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega/(2\pi)\).
This is \(q\) times their potential at its position, without a half factor: \[U_1=-\frac{q^2R}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]
The sphere surface has zero total potential, so its induced-charge potential is minus that of \(q\). The pair-energy half factor gives \(U_2=-U_1/2\), or \[U_2=\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]

\[U=U_1+U_2=-\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\] An independent derivation integrates the attractive force from infinity: \(U=-\int_d^\infty q^2Rx/[4\pi\epsilon_0(x^2-R^2)^2],dx\). Use \(\int_d^\infty x(x^2-R^2)^{-2}dx=1/[2(d^2-R^2)]\). The self-energy of the external point charge is excluded.

solution.text:
Image of a charge in a metallic object
1a. Sphere potential
Grounding fixes \(V=0\).
1b.q. Image charge
At every surface point the two potentials cancel if \(q\to q\), \(q^{\prime}=-qR/d\), and \(d^{\prime}=R^2/d\). These follow either from the two axial points or from the general surface-distance ratio.
1b.d. Image position
\(d^{\prime}=R^2/d\), lying inside the sphere.
1c. Force magnitude
The image gives an attractive force towards the centre with magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rd}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)^2}.\]
2a. Field behind the sphere
The real-charge field points towards A for positive \(q\), while the image field opposes it. Thus \[E_A=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac1{r^2}-\frac{R/d}{(r-d+R^2/d)^2}\right].\]
2b. Far field
The total charge seen at leading order is \(q+q^{\prime}=q(1-R/d)\). Therefore \[E_A\simeq\frac{q(1-R/d)}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}.\] Expanding one order further gives a correction \(-2qR(1-R^2/d^2)/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\).
2c. Complete screening
Only in the limit \(d\to R^+\), when the real and image charges coincide at the surface with opposite signs.
3a. Pendulum force
The charge-centre distance is \(s=\sqrt{l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha}\). The force points towards the sphere centre and has magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rs}{4\pi\epsilon_0(s^2-R^2)^2}.\] Draw this central force at the bob.
3b. Tangential force magnitude
Geometry gives \(\sin\gamma=l\sin\alpha/s\). The restoring-component magnitude is \[F_\perp=\frac{q^2Rl\sin\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0(l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha-R^2)^2}.\]
3c. Small-oscillation angular frequency
Linearize \(mL\ddot\alpha=-F_\perp\). The result is \[\omega=\frac{|q|}{(l-L)^2-R^2}\sqrt{\frac{Rl}{4\pi\epsilon_0mL}}.\] The ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega/(2\pi)\).
4a. External-induced interaction energy
This is \(q\) times their potential at its position, without a half factor: \[U_1=-\frac{q^2R}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]
4b. Induced-charge mutual energy
The sphere surface has zero total potential, so its induced-charge potential is minus that of \(q\). The pair-energy half factor gives \(U_2=-U_1/2\), or \[U_2=\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]
4c. Total interaction energy
\[U=U_1+U_2=-\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\] An independent derivation integrates the attractive force from infinity: \(U=-\int_d^\infty q^2Rx/[4\pi\epsilon_0(x^2-R^2)^2],dx\). Use \(\int_d^\infty x(x^2-R^2)^{-2}dx=1/[2(d^2-R^2)]\). The self-energy of the external point charge is excluded.
